scenes.text: A country wants fewer children to die before age five, and it has a fixed budget. Proposal A spends it all on health services: clinics, nurses, vaccines and medicines. Proposal B spends a third on health services, a third on clean water and sanitation, and a third on keeping girls in school to the end of secondary. Which would you fund? And here's the harder part. How could girls' education reduce child deaths? Write the steps, because there's a real mechanism.

In twenty fifteen, all one hundred and ninety-three United Nations member states adopted the Sustainable Development Goals: seventeen goals, with one hundred and sixty-nine targets, to be reached by twenty thirty. They replaced eight Millennium Development Goals, and four things changed. They apply to every country, not just poor ones, so Australia reports on itself. They're integrated, not separate. They gave the environment far more weight, and added inequality. And they promise to leave no one behind: progress must reach the most disadvantaged, not just lift the average.

Goal three is good health and well-being: healthy lives and well-being for all, at all ages. Its targets include cutting maternal and child deaths, ending epidemics like AIDS and malaria, reducing early deaths from non-communicable diseases by a third and promoting mental health, halving road traffic deaths, and universal health coverage. For Australia, the chronic disease, mental health and road targets matter most. Treat the goals as something only for other countries, and you've missed the point.

Health appears once in the goal titles, and everywhere in the mechanisms. The other goals name the determinants of health almost one by one. No poverty: income decides housing, food and whether care is delayed. Zero hunger: early nutrition shapes growth and lifelong disease risk. Clean water: diarrhoea still kills young children, and much of it is prevented by safe water and sanitation, not by clinics alone. Decent work: secure income and safe workplaces. Reduced inequalities: health follows social position. And climate action: heat, smoke and disaster. Lay them beside the determinants, and the match is close to one to one.

So here's the case for Proposal B, the SDG argument in one budget. A girl who finishes secondary school tends to have her first child later, has fewer and better-spaced pregnancies, can read health information and use vaccination services, and has more income and more say in household spending. Each step is modest, but worldwide, more education for women helps explain about half the fall in child deaths since 1970. So spending across sectors can save more children than clinics alone. That's indivisibility: the goals can't be achieved separately. It's the socio-ecological approach, written as a global agreement.

The syllabus asks how the World Health Organization applies a health lens, and it uses the goals four ways. As a measuring framework: it looks after many health indicators and publishes progress, which makes failure visible. As an argument for universal health coverage, everyone getting needed care without financial hardship. As the basis for health in all policies, where transport, housing and education departments weigh the health effects of their decisions. And for equity: leave no one behind means reporting results separately by group. But the goals aren't law. Nobody's penalised for missing them. They coordinate and make failure visible, and advocates use that.

Australia uses the goals in four ways. It reports to the United Nations through a Voluntary National Review, and keeps a national data platform. It uses them to frame aid in the Pacific and Southeast Asia, on water, health systems and education. National and state strategies are mapped to them, and national targets for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health line up with several goals. And some cities, councils, universities and organisations report against them, which is where the goals reach a local community.

Now examine it honestly. What works: one framework links health to housing, education, work and climate, and the reporting forces data split by group, which keeps gaps visible, like the gap between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians and other Australians. What's weaker: reporting is voluntary and self-assessed. Independent reviews have found Australia off track on climate and inequality. And strategies are often mapped to the goals afterwards, which changes the diagram but not the decision. The real test is whether a decision would have gone differently without the goals.
Two things to remember. One goal names health, and sixteen produce it. And the goals can't compel anyone. They coordinate, and make failure visible.
Two exam questions. First. Explain how progress on goal eleven, sustainable cities and communities, could improve the health of young Australians. Pause here to answer.

Give a mechanism, not just a link. Safe, lit public spaces and active transport make it easier for young people to be active. Affordable housing reduces crowding and stress, which protects sleep and mental health. And better public transport improves access to services, school and work. The classic mistake is saying the goal is related to health, without saying how.
Second. Examine how the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals are being used to improve health. Pause here to answer.

Describe the goals, then show health across them, with at least three goals and their mechanisms. Name real uses: WHO indicators, universal health coverage, health in all policies, and Australia's reporting. Then the limits: voluntary, self-assessed, often mapped afterwards. Conclude that they coordinate and expose, rather than compel. The classic mistake is a brochure with no limitations.

So, for any goal, trace its mechanism into health, and for any use, ask whether a decision actually changed. Next, we bring the goals down to one local community. How could they change young people's health there?
